title: Was rongorongo an independent invention of writing?
short: The undeciphered glyphs carved on about two dozen wooden objects from Rapa Nui may be a pre-contact invention of writing or a nineteenth-century response to European literacy.
matters: Writing is generally held to have been invented independently only a handful of times (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica), so a pre-contact Rapa Nui script would add a case from a small, isolated island society without cities or bureaucratic states. That would bear on theories that tie writing to administration and urbanism and on what Polynesian societies could develop in isolation. If instead the script arose after the Spanish annexation ceremony of 1770, when islanders were asked to mark a document, it would be a well-documented case of stimulus diffusion, and the question of whether the glyphs encode language at all would remain separate.
stuck: The corpus is small (fewer than 30 objects, about 15,000 glyphs in standard counts), the script ceased to be used in the 1860s after slave raids and epidemics, and nineteenth-century attempts to elicit readings from islanders produced unreliable results. Radiocarbon dates on the wood give only a terminus post quem for carving: most dated objects fall in the late eighteenth or nineteenth century, and the one fifteenth-century result (Tablet D, Échancrée) comes from non-native wood that could have been carved long after it was felled or arrived. Whether the glyphs record speech is itself disputed; claims of logosyllabic structure (Davletshin) and of a lunar calendar on Mamari (Guy) have not been converted into an agreed decipherment, and statistical tests of 'language-likeness' have been shown to misclassify non-linguistic symbol systems.
solved: Direct dates on residues or carving-associated material, or on wood from additional inscribed objects, that securely place glyph carving before 1722, combined with a reading of sign sequences that predicts Rapa Nui words or parallel passages in unseen text and outperforms matched non-linguistic controls.
approach: Compile a single, versioned digital corpus from Barthel's transcription and the newer 3D models and transcriptions (Lastilla et al.; Horley), with explicit sign-list choices recorded so that results can be rerun under alternative segmentations.

Use research agents to run statistical comparisons of rongorongo sequences against both written languages and non-linguistic symbol systems (heraldry, genealogical tallies, Polynesian tattoo and rock-art motif sequences), following Sproat's warnings about such tests, and report which conclusions survive changes in sign classification.
Test proposed readings (the Mamari lunar sequence, numeral and phonetic-complement hypotheses, parallel passages across tablets) by predicting held-out passages rather than by fitting known ones.

Extend radiocarbon and wood identification to the remaining tablets in Washington, St Petersburg, Santiago, London, Berlin and elsewhere, ideally on minimally invasive samples from carved surfaces or associated residues; this requires collaboration with the holding museums, wood anatomists and AMS radiocarbon laboratories.

title: Were Moses Shapira's Deuteronomy fragments an ancient text or an 1880s forgery?
short: Leather strips offered to Berlin and the British Museum in 1883 were dismissed as forgeries and then lost; since 2021 scholars have again argued they preserved a pre-biblical text.
matters: If the fragments were genuine, they would be by far the oldest biblical manuscript known and, on Idan Dershowitz's reading, direct evidence for a source of Deuteronomy, bearing on the composition history of the Pentateuch that critical scholarship has reconstructed only by inference. If they were forged, they are an unusually revealing case of how a nineteenth-century forger anticipated what scholars expected an ancient Hebrew text to look like, alongside the 'Moabite' pottery Shapira had sold to Berlin. The case also tests how scholarly communities judge authenticity when the object itself is lost and only copies and testimony remain.
stuck: The strips were sold at auction in 1885 and have not been traced, so no material analysis is possible. The surviving evidence consists of transcriptions, drawings and printed facsimiles of uneven accuracy, made in 1883 by Shapira, Christian David Ginsburg and others, together with expert verdicts reached in days under poor conditions. Arguments on both sides depend on whether features of the text (letter forms modelled on the Mesha stele, orthography, a variant Decalogue, a structure resembling source-critical reconstructions of Deuteronomy) are read as marks of antiquity or of a forger working from scholarship available in the 1870s.
solved: A published inventory of every linguistic, orthographic, palaeographic and textual feature in the surviving transcriptions, each classed as either attested in sources available by 1883 or first attested in material discovered later (the Dead Sea Scrolls, later Iron Age inscriptions). The question is settled for practical purposes if a set of features unavailable to an 1883 forger proves to be present, or if every feature can be traced to identifiable 1870s models.
approach: Locate, image and transcribe all surviving copies of the text: Ginsburg's papers in British Library Add MS 41294, the Shapira transcription pages Dershowitz found in the Berlin State Library, the 1883 lithographs and newspaper facsimiles, and Clermont-Ganneau's published drawings, and align them as variant witnesses.

Build a reference corpus of what a forger could have known in 1883 (the Mesha stele and its published facsimiles, the Siloam inscription, Gesenius-era grammars, the Hebrew Bible and Samaritan Pentateuch editions, source-critical studies of Deuteronomy by 1883) and test each feature of the text against it.

Compare the same features against post-1947 evidence, chiefly Qumran manuscripts of Deuteronomy and paleo-Hebrew scrolls and later Iron Age inscriptions, flagging any agreement the 1883 corpus cannot explain.

Treat the Berlin committee's report, Ginsburg's reports to the British Museum and Clermont-Ganneau's notes as testimony to be weighed, with dates, conditions of examination and what each examiner actually saw.
High-resolution digitization of British Library Add MS 41294 and the Berlin Shapira inventory, in collaboration with those libraries, is the prerequisite for a reliable critical text.

title: How much American silver reached China between 1550 and 1800?
short: Estimates of the share of Spanish American silver that ended up in China vary widely because mint, shipping and Chinese monetary records have never been reconciled in one account.
matters: The volume of silver entering China is central to the argument that world trade became global after the founding of Manila in 1571, to explanations of the Ming fiscal shift to silver, and to debates over whether a contraction of silver imports helped bring down the Ming in the 1630s–40s. It also bears on European price history, on the Dutch and English East India Companies' balance of trade, and on nineteenth-century arguments that the reversal of silver flows destabilised the Qing.
stuck: Silver reached China by several routes (the Manila galleons, the Cape route via European companies, overland through Central Asia, and from Japan, which was a larger supplier than the Americas for parts of the period), and each route is documented in different archives with different biases. Registered mint and treasury output understates production because of contraband and unregistered silver, and smuggling on the Acapulco–Manila route was extensive. Chinese sources record taxes, prices and exchange rates rather than imports, so arrivals must be inferred, and published estimates (Barrett, Flynn and Giráldez, von Glahn, TePaske) rest on different assumptions about leakage, re-export and Japanese supply.
solved: A route-by-route, decade-by-decade mass balance for 1550–1800 in which American registered production plus an explicit contraband estimate equals the sum of silver retained in the Americas, shipped to Europe, re-exported to Asia, and carried across the Pacific, with China's share derived from these flows and checked against Japanese exports and Chinese monetary indicators (silver–copper exchange rates, tax receipts in silver, price levels).
approach: Agents can assemble the published quantitative series (TePaske's mint and treasury data, Garner's mining series, VOC and East India Company bullion exports, galleon registers, Japanese export estimates) into one linked dataset with source citations and documented units, then flag gaps and double counting between routes.

Historians can specify alternative contraband and re-export assumptions and see how each changes the China total, while agents search the AGI, AGN and VOC finding aids for unused series (for example Manila customs and Acapulco registers) that would narrow the largest uncertainties.
Chinese provincial price and exchange-rate data from the Qing archives provide an independent test of the timing of inflows.

title: How much iron did Song China produce in the eleventh century?
short: Robert Hartwell's estimate of about 125,000 tons of iron in 1078 is widely repeated, but it rests on fiscal records whose relation to total output is disputed.
matters: Hartwell's figure is the main quantitative support for the idea of a Northern Song 'industrial revolution' and for claims that Chinese iron output in 1078 rivalled that of Britain in the late eighteenth century. It is used in world histories, in comparative arguments about the Great Divergence, and in environmental histories of deforestation and the shift from charcoal to coal. If output was much lower, or largely charcoal-fuelled, the narrative of a Song coal-and-iron breakthrough that later stalled needs revision.
stuck: The figure is extrapolated from iron receipts recorded for state monopoly and tax purposes in compilations such as the Song huiyao and Wenxian tongkao, which record what the state collected, not what was produced, and Hartwell's multiplier from receipts to output is an assumption. Donald Wagner argued that these administrative figures cannot be scaled up so simply, and Tim Wright's review of four decades of citation found that the estimate has been repeated far more often than tested. Archaeological evidence for Song ironworks is patchy: few smelting sites have been excavated and published in detail, and slag volumes, furnace capacities and fuel types have not been surveyed systematically.
solved: An output estimate for the 1070s, with explicit error bounds, built from at least two independent lines of evidence (the fiscal record re-read prefecture by prefecture with a stated model of collection rates, and archaeological slag-heap volumes and furnace capacities from surveyed sites), with the two lines agreeing within their stated uncertainties.
approach: Agents can extract every reference to iron production sites (ye, jian, wu), quotas and receipts from the full-text Song huiyao jigao, Xu zizhi tongjian changbian, Wenxian tongkao and Song gazetteers, map them to prefectures and dates, and assemble the competing readings of how quotas related to production.
Historians can then compare alternative collection-rate models in a single framework.

Confirmation requires collaboration with archaeometallurgists: systematic survey and volumetric measurement of slag heaps at known Song iron districts (for example around Handan and Cizhou in Hebei, and in Shanxi and Henan), radiocarbon dating of charcoal and coke inclusions, and analysis of slag and cast-iron objects (sulphur content and other tracers) to separate charcoal-fired from coal-fired production.

title: Which volcanoes caused the great unattributed sulfate spikes in polar ice, above all 1809?
short: Several of the largest volcanic sulfate deposits of the last millennium, in 1230, 1286, 1458, 1695 and 1809, have no securely identified source volcano.
matters: Reconstructions of volcanic climate forcing such as eVolv2k assign every bipolar sulfate spike without a known source to the equator, and source latitude, season and plume height change how much sulfur reached the stratosphere and how cooling was distributed between hemispheres. The 1809 event, estimated at roughly 12–19 Tg of stratospheric sulfur, opens the coldest decade of the last several centuries together with Tambora (1815); attributing it affects explanations of the harvest failures, famines and disease of the 1810s. Identifications also anchor ice-core chronologies: a named, historically dated eruption is a fixed point that can test or correct layer counting, as the reassignment of the 1450s signals to 1453 and 1458 showed.
stuck: The polar ice records the sulfate but not its origin, and the glass shards that could fingerprint a source are microscopic, scarce, and sometimes come from more than one eruption in the same layer. Many candidate volcanoes lie in regions (Melanesia, the Kurils, the Andes, island Southeast Asia) with thin written records for the relevant decades, and their deposits are poorly sampled and poorly dated. Documentary searches have tended to start from a favoured volcano and look for confirmation, and some claimed eyewitness reports have been propagated through secondary citations without checking the original source.
solved: Each spike is assigned to a named volcano by a published match between the major-element (and ideally trace-element) chemistry of glass shards in the ice layer and proximal deposits of that volcano, together with at least one dated documentary witness (an eruption report, ashfall, or optical phenomena such as a dimmed sun or abnormal twilights) consistent with the ice-core timing to within a year.
approach: Build a gazetteer-linked index of every documentary report of ashfall, dimmed or discoloured sun, dry fog, red twilights and unexplained explosions for 1228–1232, 1284–1288, 1456–1460, 1693–1697 and 1807–1810, drawing on Chinese local gazetteers (LoGaRT), Korean and Japanese court records and diaries, Arabic chronicles (OpenITI), Spanish colonial correspondence and ships' logs.

Trace every claimed witness back to the original text and edition, record the exact wording, place and date, and flag reports that rest only on secondary citations; keyword hits should be read in context, since terms for haze, halos and aurorae overlap in premodern Chinese and Japanese sources.

Score each candidate volcano listed in the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program against three tests: the timing window implied by the ice cores, the source latitude implied by the ratio of Greenland to Antarctic deposition and by sulfur isotopes, and the documentary evidence from its region.

For the leading candidates, work with tephrochronologists to sample proximal deposits, obtain radiocarbon or dendro-dated ages, and compare their glass chemistry with cryptotephra extracted from the relevant ice layers in Greenland and Antarctic cores.

title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura or other optical aids?
short: Optical effects, perspective geometry and technical imaging have been read for and against Vermeer's use of a camera obscura, with no documentary evidence either way.
matters: Vermeer is the test case for broader claims that optical projection shaped European naturalism, including the Hockney–Falco thesis, and for how far seventeenth-century Dutch painting drew on contemporary optics in Delft, the city of Leeuwenhoek. The answer bears on how his paintings were made (tracing, transfer or free construction), on attributions and chronology based on technique, and on whether instruments such as the camera obscura were working tools for painters or mainly objects of natural-philosophical interest.
stuck: No document records Vermeer owning or using an optical device, and the 1676 inventory of his household lists none. The visual evidence (halation, differential focus, perspective and scale relationships) is compatible with optical observation but can also be produced by skilled painting, and proponents and critics have relied on different paintings and different reconstructions. Recent technical imaging has shown underpainting and revisions that complicate any model of direct tracing without settling whether projection was used at some stage.
solved: A quantitative model of the geometry, scale and focus effects predicted by specific optical set-ups in a reconstructed studio, tested across all securely attributed paintings and against their underdrawings and pinhole evidence, that either fits significantly better than free-hand construction with a pin-and-string perspective or is shown to add no explanatory power.
approach: Agents can assemble a structured corpus of Vermeer's paintings with published technical imaging (infrared reflectography, MA-XRF, X-radiography, pinhole locations), extract perspective lines, object sizes and focus gradients, and test them against simulated projections from the room geometries reconstructed by Steadman and others.
A parallel search of Delft notarial, guild and Jesuit records, and of optical literature circulating in the Dutch Republic, could look for documentary links.
Confirmation needs collaboration with museum conservation scientists for access to full-resolution technical datasets and with optical engineers for physical reconstructions.

title: What do James Wilkinson's unread coded dispatches to Spanish officials say?
short: Letters between the US Army's senior general and Spanish Louisiana, written in a code keyed to an unidentified printed dictionary, remain partly or wholly unread.
matters: From 1787 James Wilkinson, later the ranking general of the US Army and governor of Louisiana Territory, took a Spanish pension and reported to the governors of Louisiana as Agent 13, so his coded letters are a running record of what Spain was told about Kentucky separatism, the Mississippi navigation question, frontier military dispositions and, later, the Burr affair. Historians have reconstructed this relationship largely from Spanish summaries, the deciphered letters that officials filed with their replies, and Wilkinson's own self-serving later accounts. Reading the undeciphered portions would show what Wilkinson actually offered, whom he named, and how Spanish policy in the Mississippi Valley responded, and it would test claims about other Americans drawn into the Spanish Conspiracy.
stuck: Much of the correspondence uses a two-part code: a numbered table of names and common words, plus page, column and row references to a printed English dictionary that neither side identified in writing and that no modern researcher has located. Chu, Valenti and Knight (2020) found that the scanned material at the Library of Congress uses at least two distinct table systems and dictionary layouts (roughly 29 versus 39 rows per column), so wordbanks from one letter do not transfer cleanly to another. Their language-model decipherment recovered about three quarters of word tokens on a held-out sample, which leaves many proper names and rare words, the content most valuable to historians, uncertain. The photostats are scattered across Spanish-archive reproduction series, and the scans used in that study are not publicly linked.
solved: A specific printed dictionary edition (or editions) is identified whose page, column and row coordinates reproduce a large set of independently known code–word pairs, including pairs withheld from the matching, and a previously unread dispatch is decoded with that key and checked against the archival original and Spanish replies.
approach: Partition the surviving coded letters by system (the table and dictionary layouts that Chu, Valenti and Knight label 1078 and 1096) before any inference, using their public transcriptions and wordbanks as a starting set and holding back a portion of known pairs for testing.

Assemble a list of English dictionaries in print between about 1760 and 1800 (pocket and spelling dictionaries, including the Entick editions associated with the separate 1806 Burr cipher) with page counts and two-column layouts, and test each edition's scanned pages from Eighteenth Century Collections Online, HathiTrust and Internet Archive for exact matches to the known page–column–row anchors, allowing for pagination offsets.

Recover the alphabetic table separately by constraining unknown table numbers between known anchors and enforcing consistency of repeated codes across all letters, and treat personal-name codes as unresolved unless an independent source confirms them.

Locate and image the manuscript pages from which the transcriptions were made, chiefly the Library of Congress photostats of Archivo General de Indias, Papeles de Cuba legajos 2373–2375, and compare against the originals in Seville; this requires collaboration with Library of Congress and AGI staff where reproductions have not been digitized.
Publish the reconstructed key with its test results and a critical edition of at least one dispatch not represented in any contemporary deciphered copy.

title: Where was Yamatai, the realm of Queen Himiko?
short: A third-century Chinese account describes the Wa polity ruled by Himiko, but its itinerary cannot be followed literally and the Kyushu and Nara candidates have been argued since the Edo period.
matters: The 'Account of the Wa' in the Wei zhi, part of Chen Shou's Sanguozhi (late third century), is the earliest substantial description of political organisation in the Japanese archipelago. If Yamatai lay in the Nara basin, a polity centred on the area that later produced the Yamato kings already led a confederation reaching to northern Kyushu by the 230s, and the first great keyhole tombs mark its rulers; if it lay in Kyushu, Yamato kingship arose separately and later, and the Wei zhi describes a regional confederation. The choice shapes accounts of state formation, of the start of the Kofun period, and of how the early chronicles Kojiki and Nihon shoki relate to the Chinese record.
stuck: Read literally, the Wei zhi's directions and travel times place Yamatai in the ocean far south of Kyushu, so every reconstruction emends either the directions (the Kinai reading turns 'south' into 'east') or the distances and order of stages (the Kyushu reading), and both sides can cite internal inconsistencies. No inscription names Yamatai or Himiko. The archaeological markers each side relies on are themselves disputed: the dates of the earliest keyhole tombs depend on radiocarbon calibration and pottery sequences, the triangular-rimmed deity-and-beast mirrors may be Wei gifts or Japanese products, and Hashihaka, the leading candidate for Himiko's tomb, is an Imperial Household Agency mausoleum closed to excavation.
solved: A set of explicitly stated readings of the Wei zhi itinerary (each with its emendations listed), each predicting where a mid-third-century paramount centre and its subordinate polities should lie, scored against the dated distribution of large settlements, mounded tombs, Chinese imports and mirrors across western Japan. The problem is solved if one reading fits the independently dated archaeological pattern much better than all others under every defensible calibration of the dates.
approach: Encode every stage of the Wei zhi itinerary and the list of subordinate countries in alternative readings (successive versus radial travel from Ito, emended directions, variant units for li and days) and compute the candidate regions each reading predicts.

Build a georeferenced database of Yayoi to early Kofun sites from the Nara National Research Institute's nationwide site-report archive: moated settlements, mounded tombs, Chinese mirrors and coins, iron, and Kibi- and Tōkai-style pottery, each with its stated date basis.

Re-model the absolute dates of the transition to the Kofun period in a single Bayesian framework that combines the Rekihaku and Makimuku radiocarbon series with dendrochronology and pottery phasing, reporting how the Hashihaka date moves under alternative calibration curves and reservoir assumptions.
Test each itinerary reading against this dated distribution and publish the scoring code so that proponents of either theory can substitute their own assumptions.

Narrowing the dates further requires collaboration with radiocarbon and dendrochronology laboratories on new short-lived samples from securely stratified contexts at Makimuku, Yoshinogari and the early Kofun mounds, and with the Imperial Household Agency for any further sampling at Hashihaka.

title: In what year did the Zhou conquer the Shang?
short: More than forty proposed dates for King Wu's victory over the last Shang king span over a century, and the official choice of 1046 BCE remains disputed.
matters: The conquest year is the pivot of early Chinese absolute chronology: the reign lengths of the Western Zhou kings are counted forward from it, and the late Shang kings, including the oracle-bone reigns at Anyang, are counted back from it. The dates of hundreds of inscribed bronzes, the calendar reconstructions they depend on, and every attempt to synchronize early China with other Bronze Age societies inherit whatever error it carries. Since 841 BCE is the earliest year fixed by continuous Chinese annalistic records, the choice of conquest year also determines how much of the preceding two centuries can be treated as dated history.
stuck: Each line of evidence fixes a date only under assumptions that the others cannot independently check: the 'current' and 'ancient' texts of the Bamboo Annals disagree with each other and with Han reckonings, the five-planet conjunction of 1059 BCE dates a portent rather than the battle, and bronze date formulas such as those on the Li gui can be fitted to many calendars depending on how lunar-phase terms are defined. Radiocarbon dates from Fengxi and Yinxu bracket the transition only to within a few decades. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (preliminary report 2000, final report 2022) chose 1046 BCE by combining these sources, but critics argued that its weighting of evidence was not transparent and that later bronze discoveries contradict its Western Zhou reign scheme.
solved: A published, reproducible model that takes every dated line of evidence as an explicit likelihood (textual reign counts, astronomical retrodictions, bronze calendar data, eclipse records, calibrated radiocarbon), returns a posterior distribution for the conquest year, and reports how that distribution shifts when each contested assumption (text version, lunar-phase definition, identification of an eclipse) is changed. The answer is settled to the extent that defensible alternative assumptions yield overlapping high-probability intervals.
approach: Compile a machine-readable corpus of all Western Zhou bronze inscriptions with full date formulas (year, month, lunar-phase term, ganzhi day) from the Academia Sinica bronze database and recent excavation reports, recording king attributions as uncertain variables.

Encode the rival interpretations of the lunar-phase terms (the four-quarters model versus Liu Xin's fixed-day model and Nivison and Shaughnessy's alternatives) and test each against the full inscription set by computing how many inscriptions each calendar can accommodate.

Retrodict the astronomical claims (the 1059 BCE conjunction, the Jupiter position implied by the Li gui and Guoyu, Shang lunar eclipses in oracle-bone inscriptions) with modern ephemerides, including uncertainty in Delta-T.

Combine these with the Bamboo Annals reign counts and the Fengxi and Yinxu radiocarbon series in a single Bayesian model (for example in OxCal or Stan), and publish the code with sensitivity runs for each contested input.

Narrowing the radiocarbon component requires collaboration with radiocarbon laboratories on new high-precision, short-lived samples from securely stratified pre- and post-conquest contexts at Fengxi and Yinxu, wiggle-matched where timber is available.

existing.note: Critique of the Project's Western Zhou chronology and of its handling of bronze and textual evidence.

existing.title: Astrology and Cosmology in Early China: Conforming Earth to Heaven
existing.note: Places the 1059 BCE conjunction and the Mandate of Heaven ideology at the centre of a broader account of early Chinese astral thought, retaining 1046 BCE.

existing.authors: David S. Nivison (ed. Adam C. Schwartz)
existing.title: The Nivison Annals: Selected Works of David S. Nivison on Early Chinese Chronology, Astronomy, and Historiography
existing.note: Collected papers, including a record of the Nivison–Shaughnessy debate on the Bamboo Annals and Nivison's later arguments for a conquest in the 1040s.

existing.title: The Xia Shang Zhou duandai gongcheng baogao and Its Chronology of the Western Zhou Dynasty
existing.note: Review of the Project's 2022 final report, arguing that bronzes published since 2000 show its Western Zhou absolute chronology to be fundamentally flawed and that the report left it uncorrected.

archives.collection: Li gui (利簋), excavated at Lintong, Shaanxi, in 1976; the only known bronze whose inscription refers directly to the conquest
archives.note: The inscription records King Wu's attack on Shang on a jiazi day and a celestial observation often read as the position of Jupiter; the object is on display and published in rubbings.

archives.repository: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, Taipei
archives.collection: Oracle bones and excavation records from the 1928–1937 Anyang (Yinxu) excavations
archives.note: Holds the excavated Shang inscriptions, including eclipse records used to fix late Shang reigns, and the field archive of the pre-war excavations.

archives.repository: Academia Sinica Digital Archives of Bronze Images and Inscriptions
archives.collection: Database of Shang and Zhou bronze inscriptions (殷周金文暨青銅器資料庫), with transcriptions, rubbings and bibliography
archives.note: Main searchable source for compiling bronze date formulas; recent finds must be added from excavation reports.

archives.collection: Yinqi wenyuan (殷契文渊) oracle-bone inscription database
archives.note: Searchable images and transcriptions of published oracle-bone inscriptions, including the lunar-eclipse records.

archives.collection: Zhushu jinian (Bamboo Annals, 'current' text) and other transmitted chronological sources
archives.note: Open full text of the current Bamboo Annals; the 'ancient text' fragments must be gathered from later quotations and modern compilations.

archives.repository: Institute of Archaeology, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Beijing
archives.collection: Excavation archives and radiocarbon dating records from Yinxu (Anyang) and Fengxi (Chang'an), including samples dated for the Chronology Project
archives.note: Holds the stratified sample series on which any refined radiocarbon estimate depends; access is by institutional collaboration.
